essays.title: Free university education
essays.prompt:
Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Whether higher education should be paid for entirely by the state is a question that divides governments and families alike. I firmly believe that tuition should be free, because the benefits of a well-educated population extend far beyond the individual graduate.

The strongest argument for free education is fairness. When fees are high, talented young people from poorer families either abandon their ambitions or begin adult life burdened by debt, while wealthier classmates face no such obstacle. Universities then reproduce existing inequality instead of reducing it. A system in which admission depends solely on ability would make far better use of a nation's talent. Germany, for instance, largely abolished tuition fees at its public universities in 2014, and its graduates remain in demand around the world.

Society as a whole also profits. Graduates generally earn more and therefore pay more tax, and vital sectors such as medicine, engineering and teaching depend on a steady supply of qualified people. Public money spent on degrees is thus an investment that is repaid over a working lifetime, not simply an expense.

Critics argue that free tuition places too heavy a burden on taxpayers, many of whom never attend university. This concern is understandable, but it can be addressed. Places can be limited to students who meet clear academic standards, and the system can be financed through progressive taxation, so that those who benefit most contribute most.
In conclusion, free university education promotes equality and strengthens the economy, and its costs can be controlled with careful planning. For these reasons, I strongly support the idea.

notes.Task Response: Clear position in the introduction, maintained throughout. The opposing view is acknowledged and answered rather than ignored. Ideas are developed with reasons and one example.
notes.Coherence: Each body paragraph opens with a clear topic sentence (strongest argument; society as a whole; critics argue). Referencing ("This concern", "Universities then") keeps paragraphs tight.
notes.Lexical Resource: Topic-specific and flexible: tuition, burdened by debt, reproduce inequality, progressive taxation. No memorised phrases.
notes.Grammar: Wide range: passive, relative clauses ("many of whom"), cleft-like emphasis ("The strongest argument... is fairness"), and "so that" result clauses, all accurate.

lang: is repaid over a working lifetime
roles: Introduction: paraphrase the question and state your position
Counter-argument, then your answer to it

essays.title: Working from home
essays.prompt:
Some people think that employees should work from home, while others believe they should work in an office. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: The rise of fast internet connections has made it possible for many people to do their jobs from home. While some see this as the future of work, others insist that the office remains essential. I will examine both positions before explaining why I favour a combination of the two.

Supporters of home working point first to flexibility. Employees save the time and money they would otherwise spend commuting, which can add up to several hours a week, and many find it easier to concentrate without the interruptions of an open-plan office. Companies benefit too, since they can employ talented people wherever they live and may spend less on office space.

However, the office has advantages that are harder to replace. Spontaneous conversations at the coffee machine often lead to new ideas, and younger staff learn a great deal simply by watching experienced colleagues at work. Furthermore, working at home blurs the line between professional and private life, and some people feel isolated or find it hard to switch off in the evening.

In my opinion, neither extreme is ideal. A hybrid arrangement, in which employees spend two or three days a week in the office and the rest at home, captures the benefits of both. Tasks that require quiet concentration can be done at home, while meetings, training and team projects are best handled face to face.

In conclusion, although remote work offers genuine freedom, the office still has an important role to play. A balanced approach is likely to be more productive and more satisfying for both employers and employees.

notes.Task Response: Both views get roughly equal space and the writer's opinion is given in the introduction ("I favour a combination") and developed in paragraph 4.
notes.Coherence: Signposting in the introduction ("I will examine both positions...") and clear contrast markers (However, Furthermore). Each paragraph deals with one view.
notes.Lexical Resource: Natural collocations: add up to, open-plan office, blur the line, switch off, face to face. Paraphrasing of "work from home" (remote work, home working).
notes.Grammar: Variety: "while" contrast, "which" non-defining clause, "in which" relative clause, "tasks that require... can be done" passive, "since" reason.

lang: are best handled face to face
roles: Introduction: both views, and a signpost to your opinion
View 1: the case for home working
View 2: the case for the office
Your own opinion, with a reason

essays.title: International tourism
essays.prompt:
International tourism has become more popular in the past few decades. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Cheaper flights and rising incomes mean that more people than ever now travel abroad. Although this growth has real drawbacks, I believe that its advantages are greater, provided that tourism is well managed.

The most obvious benefit is economic. In many countries, tourism supports millions of jobs in hotels, restaurants and transport, and it brings in foreign currency that can be used to build schools and hospitals. For small economies with few natural resources, it may be the only realistic route to prosperity. Tourism can also protect heritage: the entrance fees paid by visitors often fund the restoration of historic buildings and the protection of wildlife.

There is a cultural benefit as well. Meeting people from other countries encourages understanding and can break down stereotypes. Visitors return home with a broader outlook, and local communities gain pride in their own traditions. Some travellers even return year after year, forming lasting friendships with the people they meet.

On the other hand, the drawbacks cannot be ignored. Large numbers of visitors damage fragile environments, increase pollution and push up prices, so that residents may no longer be able to afford to live in the places where they were born. In addition, the money spent by tourists does not always stay in the local area, since many hotels and tour operators belong to foreign companies.

Nevertheless, these problems are not inevitable. Governments can limit visitor numbers, tax tourist activities and require businesses to employ local people. In conclusion, international tourism brings substantial economic and cultural gains, and with sensible regulation these gains can outweigh the harm it causes.

notes.Task Response: The question asks whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, and the answer takes a clear but conditional position ("provided that...") which is then supported.
notes.Coherence: Advantages (economic, then cultural) come before disadvantages, and the conclusion links back to the introduction. "On the other hand" and "Nevertheless" mark the turns in the argument.
notes.Lexical Resource: Less common but natural items: heritage, fragile environments, push up prices, foreign currency, route to prosperity.
notes.Grammar: Comparatives, "provided that", "so that" with modal, and a "since" clause. Passive and reduced relative clauses ("paid by visitors") appear without forcing.

roles: Introduction: your position, with a condition
Answer to the question: conditions and conclusion

essays.title: Rising obesity
essays.prompt:
In many countries, the number of people who are overweight is increasing. What are the causes of this problem, and what can be done to solve it?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Excess weight has become one of the most serious health concerns of the modern world, affecting both rich and poor countries. This essay will consider the main causes of the trend and suggest several practical solutions.

The first cause is a change in diet. Processed food that is high in sugar and fat is cheap, heavily advertised and available almost everywhere, so it has replaced home-cooked meals in many households. Portion sizes have also grown, and people often eat without noticing how much they have consumed. The second cause is a more inactive lifestyle. Many jobs now involve sitting at a desk for hours, and cars and screens have reduced the amount of walking and play that earlier generations took for granted.

There are several ways to tackle these problems. Governments could place a tax on sugary drinks, as some countries have already done, and restrict the advertising of unhealthy products to children. They could also require clear labels showing the calorie content of food, which would help consumers to make informed choices.

Education is equally important. Schools should teach children how to cook simple, healthy meals and should guarantee daily physical activity, so that good habits are formed early. At the same time, cities can encourage exercise by building safe cycle lanes and public parks. Employers, for their part, could offer gym membership or allow staff to take active breaks.

In conclusion, rising weight is the result of unhealthy eating and a lack of movement. By combining sensible regulation with education and better urban planning, societies can help people to live healthier lives.

notes.Task Response: Both parts of the question are answered fully: two causes in paragraph 2, two groups of solutions in paragraphs 3 and 4. Nothing is exaggerated or unsupported.
notes.Coherence: The structure mirrors the question (causes, then solutions). Ordinal markers (first, second), "equally important" and "for their part" are natural, not mechanical.
notes.Lexical Resource: Accurate collocations: processed food, portion sizes, took for granted, tackle problems, make informed choices, active breaks.
notes.Grammar: Modals for suggestion (could, should), present perfect for change (have grown, have reduced), "which" referring to a whole clause, and relative clauses.

lang: so that good habits are formed
roles: Introduction: the problem and what the essay will do

essays.title: Children and smartphones
essays.prompt:
Many children now spend several hours a day using smartphones. Why is this happening? Is it a positive or a negative development?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Smartphones have become a normal part of childhood in many parts of the world. In my view, this trend is driven by a combination of convenience and peer pressure, and on balance it is more harmful than helpful.

There are several reasons why children spend so long on their phones. Firstly, the devices are cheap, portable and packed with entertainment, from games to short videos that are designed to keep users watching. Secondly, parents who work long hours often use phones to keep their children occupied, or to stay in contact with them. Finally, social life now takes place online, so a child without a phone may feel excluded from friendships.

Admittedly, there are some benefits. Phones give children immediate access to information, and educational apps can make learning more engaging. Used sensibly, they also allow families to stay in touch and help young people to learn technical skills that will be valuable in the future. For older children in particular, a phone can also provide reassurance about safety on the journey to school.

However, I believe that the disadvantages are more serious. Prolonged screen time reduces the hours that children spend on exercise, face-to-face conversation and sleep, all of which are essential for healthy development. It may also shorten their attention span, since constant notifications train the brain to expect quick rewards. Moreover, unsupervised access exposes children to inappropriate content and online bullying.

In conclusion, although smartphones have educational and social benefits, the amount of time children spend on them is a cause for concern. Parents and schools should set clear limits so that technology serves children rather than controls them.

notes.Task Response: The two questions (why, and positive or negative) are answered separately, and the opinion ("more harmful than helpful") is clear from the first paragraph.
notes.Coherence: Reasons are listed with Firstly / Secondly / Finally; the counter-argument is introduced by "Admittedly" and rejected by "However". The conclusion repeats the position in new words.
notes.Lexical Resource: Peer pressure, keep them occupied, attention span, inappropriate content, prolonged screen time. Paraphrase of "smartphones" (devices, phones) avoids repetition.
notes.Grammar: Relative clauses ("all of which are essential"), passive participle ("designed to keep users watching"), and "so that" purpose clause at the end.

roles: Introduction: answer both questions in outline
Question 2: why it is mainly negative

essays.title: School uniforms
essays.prompt:
Some people think that students should wear a uniform at school. Others believe that students should be free to choose what they wear. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Few topics divide teachers, parents and students as reliably as school uniforms. Although there are sound reasons for requiring them, I believe that students should generally be allowed to choose their own clothes, within sensible limits.

Those in favour of uniforms usually begin with equality. When everyone dresses the same, differences in family income are less visible, and pupils are less likely to be teased for wearing cheaper clothes. Uniforms also save time and money, because families do not have to buy fashionable outfits every season and students do not have to decide what to wear each morning. In addition, a uniform can create a sense of belonging, which many schools hope will improve discipline and school spirit.

On the other hand, there are strong arguments for freedom of choice. Clothing is one of the main ways in which young people express their personalities, and allowing them to do so can build confidence and creativity. Uniforms can also be uncomfortable or unsuitable, for example in hot weather, and they cost parents a considerable sum if the school requires an expensive, specific brand.

Weighing up these points, I think that the benefits of uniforms are real but overstated. Bullying over clothing can be reduced through a simple dress code, which bans offensive slogans and very expensive items, while still giving students a degree of choice. Moreover, schools that rely on uniforms to produce discipline are ignoring the more important influence of good teaching and clear rules.
In conclusion, a flexible dress code seems preferable to a strict uniform. It protects equality without suppressing individuality.

notes.Task Response: Both sides are discussed in full, and the writer takes a moderate but clear position, offering a middle solution (a dress code) rather than a vague "both are good".
notes.Coherence: The first body paragraph builds around "equality", the second around "freedom". The opinion paragraph uses a weighing phrase (Weighing up these points) to move from discussion to judgement.
notes.Lexical Resource: School spirit, sense of belonging, teased, dress code, suppress individuality, overstated. Nothing is overly formal or memorised.
notes.Grammar: Contrast with "Although", passive modals, relative clauses with prepositions ("ways in which"), and a participle phrase ("Weighing up these points").

roles: Introduction: both views and your leaning
View 2: the case for free choice
Your own opinion: weigh the points and offer a solution

essays.title: Traffic in big cities
essays.prompt:
Traffic congestion is a serious problem in many large cities. What problems does it cause, and what measures could be taken to reduce it?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: As cities grow, roads that were built for far fewer vehicles are struggling to cope. This essay will outline the main consequences of congestion and propose measures that could ease it.

Congestion affects individuals, businesses and the environment. Commuters lose hours every week sitting in traffic, which causes stress and leaves less time for family and rest. Companies suffer as well, because deliveries are delayed and employees arrive late, and the resulting loss of productivity is costly for the whole economy. Furthermore, vehicles that move slowly or stand still produce more exhaust fumes, which worsens air quality and harms public health.

The most effective long-term solution is to offer a better alternative to the private car. Investment in metro lines, trams and reliable bus services would persuade many people to leave their cars at home, provided that fares are affordable and routes serve the places that people actually need to reach. Safe cycle lanes and wide pavements would encourage short journeys on foot or by bike.

In the meantime, governments can use regulation to discourage unnecessary driving. Charging drivers to enter the city centre at peak hours has reduced traffic in several major cities, and the revenue can be used to improve public transport. Employers could also be encouraged to introduce flexible hours or home working, so that fewer people travel at the same time.
To sum up, traffic jams waste time, damage the economy and pollute the air. A combination of better public transport and sensible restrictions on car use offers the best hope of solving the problem.

notes.Task Response: Both problems and measures are covered, with problems organised by who is affected (individuals, business, environment) and measures by time frame (long-term, short-term).
notes.Coherence: Logical grouping makes the essay easy to follow. "In the meantime" shows a deliberate change from long-term to immediate measures.
notes.Lexical Resource: Congestion, exhaust fumes, loss of productivity, peak hours, revenue, flexible hours. Accurate and appropriate for the topic.
notes.Grammar: Conditional modals (would persuade, would encourage), "provided that", present perfect for evidence ("has reduced traffic"), and defining/non-defining relative clauses.

lang: a better alternative to the private car
roles: Introduction: the problem and what the essay will do

essays.title: Languages in primary school
essays.prompt:
Some people say that children should begin learning a foreign language in primary school rather than secondary school. Do you agree or disagree?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: At what age should children begin to study a foreign language? Some educators argue that secondary school is early enough, but I strongly agree that lessons should start in primary school.

The main reason is that young children learn languages more naturally. Their brains are flexible, and they are less afraid of making mistakes than teenagers, who are often embarrassed to speak in front of classmates. Children who begin early are also more likely to develop a good accent and to understand the sounds and rhythm of the language, which is much harder to achieve later in life. Many families in multilingual countries show that children can acquire a second or third language with surprising ease.

In addition, an early start gives learners more time. A language needs thousands of hours of exposure to master, and a student who starts at seven has several more years of practice than one who starts at twelve. By the time they reach secondary school, such pupils can already communicate and can spend their lessons reading, writing and discussing more complex topics.

It is sometimes argued that primary schools should concentrate on reading, writing and mathematics, and that an additional subject would overload young children. However, language lessons in the early years do not need to be formal. Songs, stories and games can make them enjoyable, and research suggests that learning a second language can even strengthen a child's skills in the first.

In conclusion, starting a foreign language in primary school makes learning easier, gives pupils more time and need not add pressure. I therefore believe that it should be part of the curriculum from the first years of education.

notes.Task Response: The writer states a strong position in the introduction and answers the main counter-argument (overload) before concluding. "Research suggests" is used instead of invented statistics.
notes.Coherence: Reason one is quality of learning, reason two is quantity of time; paragraph 4 refutes the objection. Cohesive devices such as "In addition" and "However" are accurate and not overused.
notes.Lexical Resource: Exposure, acquire, multilingual, overload, curriculum, with ease. Word choice is precise and the topic is paraphrased (foreign language, second language, language lessons).
notes.Grammar: Embedded questions, comparatives ("more naturally", "much harder"), passive constructions ("It is sometimes argued that"), and a "need not" modal form.

roles: Introduction: paraphrase the question and state your position
Counter-argument, then your answer to it

essays.title: Studying abroad
essays.prompt:
More and more students choose to study at universities abroad. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this trend?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: It is increasingly common for young people to leave their home country to earn a degree overseas. While this experience has certain drawbacks, I believe that its benefits are more substantial.

The first advantage is educational. Students can gain access to universities and courses that are not available at home, and they often study in a language that will be valuable throughout their careers. Living abroad also develops independence: managing money, cooking and solving practical problems without parental help builds maturity far more quickly than staying at home. Some foreign universities also offer better research facilities and more flexible courses than those available locally.

A second benefit lies in the experience of other cultures. Students meet classmates from many countries, which broadens their outlook and helps them to build an international network of contacts. Employers often look favourably on graduates who have shown that they can adapt to a different environment.

Nevertheless, studying overseas is not without risks. The most obvious is cost, since tuition fees and living expenses are generally higher than at home, and not every family can afford them. Loneliness and homesickness are also common, especially in the first months, and some students struggle to adjust to the climate, food or teaching style. A further concern for countries that send students abroad is that the most talented may decide not to return, which can lead to a loss of skills.

In conclusion, although studying abroad can be expensive and emotionally demanding, the academic, personal and professional gains are considerable. For students who are well prepared and supported, it is likely to be a rewarding investment.

notes.Task Response: Both sides of the trend are discussed and the writer gives a judgement. A different angle (the country that loses talent) shows a wider view than only the student's.
notes.Coherence: Advantages come first and take two paragraphs; disadvantages are balanced in one longer paragraph. Topic sentences (The first advantage, A second benefit, Nevertheless) lead each section.
notes.Lexical Resource: Earn a degree, broadens their outlook, look favourably on, adjust to, homesickness, emotionally demanding. Natural and varied.
notes.Grammar: Gerund subjects (Living abroad also develops...), relative clauses referring to whole ideas ("which broadens"), and a final conditional-style structure with "likely to be".

essays.title: Do we still need libraries?
essays.prompt:
Some people say that public libraries are no longer necessary because information is available on the internet. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Now that most information can be found online in seconds, some argue that public libraries have become obsolete. I strongly disagree, because libraries do far more than lend books, and many of their services cannot be replaced by a search engine.

First, libraries provide equal access. Not everyone owns a computer or can afford a reliable internet connection, and for these people a library is often the only place where they can look for jobs, complete school assignments or fill in official forms. In a world where so much depends on being online, closing libraries would widen the gap between those who have technology and those who do not.

Libraries also offer something that the internet struggles to provide: reliable, organised knowledge and guidance. Online, a student may find thousands of conflicting pages on a single topic, many of them inaccurate. A librarian can direct that student to trustworthy sources and teach the skills needed to judge them. Furthermore, a quiet reading room gives children and adults a space for concentration that is hard to find at home, away from notifications and distractions.

It could be objected that e-books and digital archives make physical buildings unnecessary and that the money would be better spent elsewhere. This view overlooks how libraries have adapted. Many now lend e-books, host free courses and run activities for children and elderly residents, so they function as community centres as well as stores of books. Their cost is modest compared with the social benefit they bring.

In conclusion, the internet has changed how we find information, but it has not removed the need for libraries. They give everyone equal access, guide people to reliable knowledge and bring communities together, so they deserve continued public support.

notes.Task Response: A strong position ("I strongly disagree") is given at once and defended with two reasons that are different in kind (equal access; quality and guidance). The objection is stated fairly and answered.
notes.Coherence: Each paragraph begins with a signpost (First; also; It could be objected). "This view" and "Their cost" refer back precisely, so no idea floats free.
notes.Lexical Resource: Obsolete, equal access, widen the gap, trustworthy sources, community centres. Paraphrases "internet" as "online" and "search engine" rather than repeating the word.
notes.Grammar: Passive modal ("It could be objected that"), reduced relative ("conflicting pages"), result clause with "so", and comparisons.

roles: Introduction: paraphrase the question and state your position
Counter-argument, then your answer to it

essays.title: Practical skills at school
essays.prompt:
Some people think that schools should teach practical skills such as cooking, basic repairs and managing money. Others believe that schools should concentrate on academic subjects. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Education systems have long concentrated on subjects such as mathematics, science and languages. Recently, however, many parents and employers have called for lessons in practical life skills. This essay will discuss both positions, but I believe that the two can be combined.

Those who favour academic subjects argue that the main purpose of school is to develop the mind. Mathematics, history and literature teach analysis, memory and clear expression, which are useful in almost any career, and a crowded timetable could reduce the time available for them. Practical skills, they add, can be learnt at home from parents at little cost to the school.

Supporters of practical lessons reply that not every family is able or willing to teach these skills. A young adult who cannot prepare a simple meal, draw up a budget or understand a rental contract may struggle to live independently, however well they performed in examinations. Money management is a particularly strong example: many graduates leave education without understanding loans or interest rates, and so make costly decisions. Practical subjects can also motivate students who find traditional lessons less engaging, since they can see an immediate use for what they are learning.

In my view, schools should offer both. A small number of hours each week, perhaps one afternoon, would be enough to cover cooking, first aid and personal finance without damaging academic standards. Indeed, some practical activities, such as calculating the cost of ingredients, reinforce mathematics rather than competing with it.
In conclusion, academic subjects remain the core of education, but practical lessons prepare young people for real life. A balanced timetable can provide both.

notes.Task Response: Both views are presented in their strongest form, then the writer gives a reasoned middle position with a concrete proposal (one afternoon a week).
notes.Coherence: The reply structure is clear: view one, then "Supporters... reply", which makes paragraph 3 answer paragraph 2 directly. Opinion is not hidden until the end.
notes.Lexical Resource: Academic subjects, life skills, draw up a budget, interest rates, engaging, personal finance. Words are precise and not exotic.
notes.Grammar: Concessive "however well they performed", relative clauses, "since" reason clause, and "rather than competing" participle structure.

roles: Introduction: both views, and a signpost to your opinion
Your own opinion, with a concrete proposal

essays.title: Shopping online
essays.prompt:
More and more people are buying goods online instead of in shops. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Online shopping has grown so quickly that, for many people, visiting a shop is now the exception rather than the rule. Although this trend has drawbacks for communities, I believe that its benefits for consumers and businesses are greater.

The first advantage is convenience. Shoppers can compare prices, read reviews and place an order at any hour, without travelling or queuing, which saves time and fuel. This is especially valuable for people who are elderly, disabled or live far from large towns, and who may otherwise find it hard to buy basic goods. Competition between websites also tends to keep prices low, so that families on limited budgets can buy more for their money.

Online selling benefits businesses as well. A small company can reach customers in other regions or countries without renting an expensive shop, which allows new entrepreneurs to start with little capital. In this way, the internet has made the market more open.

There are, nevertheless, genuine disadvantages. High-street shops are closing as customers move online, and this means job losses and empty town centres. Buyers cannot touch or try a product before purchase, so returns are common, and parcel delivery adds to traffic and packaging waste. There is also the risk of fraud and the misuse of personal data.

These problems can, however, be reduced. Local authorities can support town centres by lowering business taxes and encouraging shops to offer experiences that cannot be copied online, while stricter regulation can protect consumers. In conclusion, the convenience, choice and lower prices of online shopping outweigh its drawbacks, provided that governments act to manage the consequences.

notes.Task Response: The question is "do the advantages outweigh": the answer is yes, with a condition, and the essay then proves it by covering consumers, businesses, and the main harms.
notes.Coherence: Advantages to consumers, then to businesses, then disadvantages, then an answer to those disadvantages. The last paragraph both rebuts and concludes, which keeps the essay within 280 words.
notes.Lexical Resource: The exception rather than the rule, high-street shops, limited budgets, little capital, packaging waste, misuse of personal data.
notes.Grammar: Reduced adjective clauses, "so that" result, "provided that", and "which" referring to a whole clause.

lang: the exception rather than the rule

essays.title: Graduates and jobs
essays.prompt:
In many countries, young people find it hard to get a job after finishing their studies. What are the causes of this problem, and what can be done to solve it?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Finishing a degree or diploma is supposed to be the start of a career, yet in many countries graduates spend months or even years searching for work. This essay will examine the main reasons for the difficulty and suggest practical ways to improve the situation.

One important cause is a mismatch between education and the labour market. Universities often teach theory, while employers want candidates who already have practical experience and skills such as teamwork, communication and the use of current software. As a result, many graduates are qualified on paper but unprepared for the workplace. A second cause is competition. When the economy slows down, companies hire fewer new staff and prefer experienced workers, so young people with no work history are the first to be turned away.

Several measures could help. Universities should cooperate with employers to design courses that include internships, projects with real companies and training in practical skills. Students who have spent a few months in a workplace before graduating are far more attractive to recruiters.

Governments can also play a role. They could give companies tax benefits for hiring young people and offer small grants to graduates who wish to start their own business. Career guidance, provided early in secondary school, would help young people to choose subjects for which there is genuine demand, and regular publication of data on which sectors are growing would make those choices better informed.

In conclusion, graduate unemployment results from a gap between education and employers' needs, together with fierce competition for limited jobs. Closer links between universities and companies, supported by sensible government policy, can make the transition from study to work much easier.

notes.Task Response: Two clear causes and two groups of solutions, one aimed at universities and one at governments. Each solution answers a cause, which shows the writer is solving the stated problem and not a general one.
notes.Coherence: Cause paragraphs mirror solution paragraphs. Phrases like "A second cause" and "Governments can also" make the structure easy to follow.
notes.Lexical Resource: Mismatch, labour market, internships, recruiters, tax benefits, career guidance, fierce competition.
notes.Grammar: Participle phrases ("provided early in secondary school"), "for which" relative clause, comparative "far more attractive", and passive infinitive ("to be turned away").

lang: the first to be turned away
for which there is genuine demand
the transition from study to work
roles: Introduction: the problem and what the essay will do

essays.title: Moving to the city
essays.prompt:
In many countries, more and more people are moving from rural areas to cities. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Urbanisation is one of the defining trends of our time, with more than half of the world's population now living in cities. This essay will explain the main reasons for the movement and argue that it is a positive development overall, although it brings serious challenges.

People move to cities mainly in search of work. Rural economies often depend on farming, which offers limited and uncertain incomes, whereas cities contain factories, offices and service industries that provide a wider range of jobs and higher wages. Education and healthcare are another attraction, since the best universities and hospitals are usually concentrated in urban areas. Finally, many young people are drawn by the social life that a large city offers, and once relatives have settled there, others tend to follow.

There are clear benefits to this trend. Cities are centres of innovation and economic growth, as businesses and talented people gain from being close to one another. Services can also be supplied more efficiently to a dense population: it is cheaper to provide a hospital, a school or a bus network for a million people in one place than for the same number scattered over a large area.

However, rapid urban growth can cause problems. Housing becomes expensive, and in some countries newcomers live in overcrowded settlements without proper sanitation. Traffic and pollution increase, while villages lose their young and energetic residents and the elderly are left behind.

On balance, though, I believe that these problems can be managed through planning, such as affordable housing and public transport, and through investment in rural areas to slow the exodus. In conclusion, people move to cities for work, services and opportunity, and, with good management, this migration can benefit both the economy and individuals.

notes.Task Response: The two questions get a paragraph each (why; positive or negative), with the position announced in the introduction. The negative side is conceded and answered, not ignored.
notes.Coherence: The reasons are grouped (work, services, social life). The final paragraph returns to the opening position ("On balance, though").
notes.Lexical Resource: Urbanisation, defining trend, uncertain incomes, concentrated in urban areas, overcrowded settlements, exodus.
notes.Grammar: "whereas" contrast, "once relatives have settled" time clause, "it is cheaper to... than for..." comparison, and passive "are left behind".

lang: one of the defining trends of our time
roles: Introduction: answer both questions in outline

essays.title: Living longer
essays.prompt:
People in many countries are living longer than before. Why is this happening? What problems might it cause for society?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model: Life expectancy has risen dramatically over the last century, and in many countries it now exceeds eighty years. This essay will outline the main causes of this change and discuss the challenges it creates for society.

The most important cause is progress in medicine and public health. Vaccines and antibiotics have defeated diseases which once killed millions, and modern surgery and drugs allow people to survive and manage conditions such as heart disease. Improvements in daily life have also contributed. Clean drinking water, better sanitation and safer housing prevent infection, while a more reliable food supply has reduced malnutrition. In addition, greater awareness of healthy habits, such as exercise and not smoking, helps people to remain well in old age.

The first problem is financial. As the number of retired people grows and the number of workers falls, governments must pay more in pensions and healthcare with a smaller tax base. This may force them to raise taxes, increase the retirement age or reduce benefits, all of which are unpopular.

A second problem concerns care. Older people are more likely to need long-term medical and social support, and many countries do not have enough nurses, carers or suitable housing. Families, who traditionally looked after elderly relatives, may no longer be able to do so because they live far away or both parents work. There is also a risk of loneliness among the elderly, which damages both physical and mental health.

In conclusion, medical advances, cleaner living conditions and healthier lifestyles explain why people live longer, but an ageing population puts pressure on public finances and care services. Governments need to plan early, for example by encouraging flexible retirement and investing in community care.

notes.Task Response: Both questions are answered fully: one developed paragraph of causes (medical, environmental, lifestyle) and two of problems (financial, care). A short recommendation in the conclusion adds value without adding a new argument.
notes.Coherence: The sequence "The first problem... A second problem..." is clear. Each paragraph has one controlling idea and supporting detail.
notes.Lexical Resource: Life expectancy, public health, malnutrition, tax base, retirement age, long-term support, community care.
notes.Grammar: Present perfect for change over time, "which once killed millions", "all of which are unpopular", and a "by + -ing" recommendation.

roles: Introduction: what the essay will cover

principles: Plan for 5 minutes, write for 30, check for 5. A plan with a position and two or three reasons stops you rambling.
Aim for 260 to 290 words. Under 250 loses marks; 350 words usually means more errors, not more marks.
Four paragraphs is enough, five is better when the question has two parts. Each paragraph carries one controlling idea.
Every sentence has a job: state, explain, give an example, or link. If you cannot name its job, cut it.
Answer the exact question. If it asks "to what extent", give a position. If it asks for causes and solutions, give both.
Paraphrase the question in your introduction instead of copying it. Then state your position or outline in one sentence.
Use examples from general knowledge or experience, kept short. Never invent statistics: write "research suggests" or give no figure.
Make your position the same in the introduction and the conclusion.

types.name: Opinion (agree or disagree)
asks: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Do you agree or disagree with this statement?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase, then say clearly whether you agree, disagree or partly agree
Body 1: your strongest reason, explained and illustrated
Body 2: a second, different reason
Optional: the opposite view and why you reject it
Conclusion: restate your position in new words
tips: Choose one position and keep it. A clear "I strongly agree" beats a vague "both sides".
If you partly agree, say which part in the introduction and keep that balance throughout.
Two well-developed reasons are better than four thin ones.
traps: Writing about the topic in general and never about the exact statement.

types.name: Discussion (both views + opinion)
asks: Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Some people think A. Others think B. Discuss both views.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both views and say what you think
Body 1: the first view, with reasons
Body 2: the second view, with reasons
Your opinion: weigh the views and justify
Conclusion: short summary
tips: Give both views a fair hearing: roughly equal space.
The phrase "give your opinion" is not optional. Put it in the introduction and develop it.
Present each view as its supporters would, not as a weak argument you plan to destroy.
traps: Describing only one view in detail.
Hiding your opinion until the last sentence.
Using "some people say" for everything without ever explaining why.

types.name: Advantages and disadvantages
asks: What are the advantages and disadvantages?
Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase and (if asked) state which side is stronger
Body 1: advantages, one or two, with detail
Body 2: disadvantages, one or two, with detail
Optional: how the drawbacks can be reduced
Conclusion: weigh the two sides
tips: If the question says "outweigh", answer it: the advantages do, the disadvantages do, or neither clearly.
Spend more words on the side you think is stronger.
Keep advantages together and disadvantages together. Do not zigzag.
traps: Using the same example for both sides.

types.name: Problem and solution
asks: What are the causes of this problem and what can be done?
What problems does this cause and how can they be solved?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase the problem and outline the essay
Body 1: causes (or effects), each explained
Body 2: solutions, each linked to a cause
Optional: a second group of solutions (who does what)
Conclusion: summarise problem and best solutions
tips: Match each solution to a cause so the essay feels logical.
Say who should act: government, schools, employers, individuals.
Be realistic. "Ban all cars" is easy to criticise; "congestion charges" is not.
traps: Solutions that have nothing to do with the causes you gave.
Only one cause and one solution, both undeveloped.
Vague phrases such as "the government must do something".

types.name: Two-part question
asks: Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
What are the reasons for this? What problems might it cause?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase and outline your answer to both questions
Body 1: answer question 1 fully
Body 2: answer question 2 fully
Optional: concession or second part of question 2
Conclusion: give a short answer to both again
tips: Answer each question in its own paragraph(s). Do not blend them.
When the second question asks for a judgement (positive or negative), give one and defend it.
Underline the question words ("why", "is it positive") before planning.
traps: Answering only one of the two questions.
Giving a list of reasons with no development.

lessons.title: Read the question before the topic
intro: A Band 9 essay answers the exact question, not the general subject. Most lost marks at this level come from writing a good essay about the wrong thing.
A Task 2 question reaches you in one of three shapes. Learn to recognise each one in seconds.
points: Two views are given
Some people say homework should be banned, while others think it is essential. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
You must cover both views and say what you think.
A direct question
Should schools teach students how to manage money, or is that a job for parents?
Answer the question itself. A "should" question needs a clear answer in your introduction.
A single statement
Handwriting is no longer a useful skill. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Respond to this claim, not to "handwriting" in general. Decide your position first.
steps: Underline the instruction words (discuss, to what extent, what are the causes).
Circle the topic words and think of two synonyms for each. You will need them for paraphrasing.
Count the tasks: one question or two? Both views or one claim?
Write your answer to the question in one sentence. That sentence is your position, and it goes in the introduction.

lessons.title: Open with one precise sentence
intro: The first sentence should place the reader inside the topic. It should be specific enough that nobody could paste it into an essay on a different subject.
Avoid three things: sweeping statements about history or the modern world, claims so obvious that no one could argue with them, and memorised frames that you drop an idea into.
steps: Name the topic with a concrete detail: a trend, a change, or a tension between two groups.
Link that detail to the question without copying its words.
Finish the introduction with your position or a one-line outline of what you will do.
pairs: Throughout history, humans have always used transport and it is very important in our lives.
Over the past decade, many cities have started charging drivers to enter their centres, a move that supporters praise and critics resent.
The second sentence gives a real development and shows why the question is worth debating.
It is clear to everybody that education is good, so schools matter.
Parents and employers increasingly ask schools to teach more than exam subjects, and opinions differ on how far schools should go.
The first sentence states something nobody disputes and says nothing about the question.
In this modern world, social media is a very important topic that many people discuss.
Teenagers now spend several hours a day on social media, and this has made parents and teachers anxious about its effects.
"In this modern world" is filler. A fact about teenagers and a reaction to it is real content.

lessons.title: Connect your paragraphs
intro: A new paragraph tells the reader that one point is finished and another begins. A good first sentence also shows how the two are related, and it does so in very few words.
Test your essay by reading only the first sentence of each paragraph. If the argument still makes sense, the essay is well built. If it does not, the paragraphs are not doing their jobs.
points: Adding a point
A second reason is that... / A further factor is...
Signals the same direction.
Changing direction
However, critics point out that... / On the other hand, ...
Signals a contrast with the paragraph before.
Following a cause with a result
As a consequence, ... / This has led to...
Signals that the new paragraph follows logically.
Moving to solutions
In response to these problems, ... / Several measures could help.
Signals a change of task inside the essay.
steps: Pick the link-back word: This, These, Such, Another, A further, A second.
Add a summary noun that captures the previous idea: trend, factor, development, approach, view, concern, claim, policy, change, measure, issue.
Say what the new paragraph is about. Example pattern: "This trend [link-back], however, [contrast] has an impact on small shops [new topic]."
Avoid starting every paragraph with First, Second, Third. Mix it up.
pairs: Cars are expensive. Many people cannot afford them. Cars cause pollution. Fares are rising.
Rising fares have pushed many commuters back to their cars. This trend worsens both congestion and pollution.
"This trend" packs the whole previous sentence into two words, so you can move on to the effect.

lessons.title: Say more with fewer words: nouns
intro: Academic writing often turns an action into a noun. A long clause becomes a short phrase, and the sentence says the same thing in fewer words. This is what examiners mean when they praise "range of structures" and "precision".
The method is simple: find the verb, change it into a noun, and give it a new verb that links cause and result (lead to, result in, contribute to, reduce, increase).
steps: Find the verbs in your sentence.
Change one or two into nouns: increase to an increase in, decide to a decision, improve to an improvement in, rely to reliance on, depend to dependence on.
Add a linking verb: leads to, results in, contributes to, reduces.
Stop when the sentence is clear. Three nouns in a row is usually too many.
pairs: When prices rise, people buy less food.
A rise in prices reduces food purchases.
Eight words become six, and the sentence has the formal tone of a report.
If the government spends more on schools, teachers can offer better lessons.
Increased investment in schools improves the quality of teaching.
Two clauses become one subject plus one verb.
Because people use their phones too much, they sleep badly.
Excessive phone use contributes to poor sleep.
The noun phrase "excessive phone use" replaces a whole clause.

lessons.title: Cautious language (hedging)
intro: In an essay you rarely have evidence for large claims. Careful writers soften what they cannot prove and stay firm about what they can. This gives balance and also protects you from saying something false.
Hedging is not weakness. Overdo it and your sentences become vague, so use it where it is needed.
points: Soften general claims
may, might, can, could, tends to, appears to, is likely to
Smartphones may reduce concentration. Experts suggest that...
Limit the scope
some, many, most, often, in some cases, to some extent
Some teenagers... / Many employers...
Refer to evidence you do not name
Research suggests that, There is evidence that, It is widely believed that
Use these instead of inventing statistics.
Do NOT hedge
facts, definitions, and your own position
"I strongly believe..." not "I perhaps tend to think..."
steps: Read each sentence that makes a claim about people or society.
Ask: could I prove this word for word? If not, soften it.
Keep your position sentence confident.
Be diplomatic about the other side: "This view is understandable, but..." is better than "This is stupid."
pairs: Video games make children aggressive.
Violent video games may increase aggressive behaviour in some children.
The first sentence is a sweeping claim that nobody can prove.
Young people never read books.
Fewer young people than in the past read books for pleasure.
Swap an absolute (never) for a comparison you could defend.

lessons.title: Efficiency: cut what does not work
intro: Your aim is 260 to 290 words in which every sentence has a job. Extra words do not add marks, but they do add errors and use up time.
The word count in the exam is a minimum. Reach it with ideas, not with padding.
steps: Cut filler openings: in this modern world, as we all know, it goes without saying.
Cut repetition: future plans, very unique, advance planning, my own personal opinion.
Replace long phrases with one word: in order to to simply to, due to the fact that to because.
If two sentences make the same point, keep the better one and use the saved words for an example.
pairs: In my personal opinion, I think that it is a very important thing that governments should plan for the future in advance.
Governments should plan ahead.
17 words become 4, and nothing is lost.
Due to the fact that many people are unemployed, there are many problems in society.
Because many people are unemployed, society suffers.
The meaning is the same in half the length.

lessons.title: Five-minute plan
intro: Spending five minutes planning is the best use of your time in the exam. A plan prevents the most expensive mistakes: no clear position, repeated ideas, and a conclusion that contradicts the introduction.
steps: Minute 1: underline the instruction words, circle the topic, decide your position.
Minutes 2 to 3: write two or three main ideas as short phrases, not sentences. For each idea add a reason or example.
Minute 4: choose the paragraph order. Put your strongest idea first, or last if you want to end with force.
Minute 5: write your first sentence and the first sentence of each paragraph. The rest will follow.
Brainstorming questions that always work: Who is affected? What changes? What is the cost? What would happen if nobody acted?

lessons.title: Final five-minute check
intro: Most candidates make the same small errors again and again. A planned check removes most of them.
steps: Does the introduction answer the question? Does the conclusion repeat the same answer in new words?
Does every paragraph start with a clear topic sentence?
Subjects and verbs: does each verb agree with its subject (people are, the number of students is)?
Articles and plurals: a / the / no article; one problem, two problems.
Is the spelling consistent (British or American, not both)? Are numbers and names correct?
Count your words. Cross out anything repeated rather than adding new sentences at the end.
